title: Ekphrasis I
content:
Image Gallery 1 / 1
Image of Achilles’ shield from The Iliad (translated by Pope), pg 171 of Vol. 5, published in 1720. The Shield of Achilles by John Flaxman (1821-22) PREVIOUS NEXT The Shield of Achilles
Homer, Iliad 18.478–608
First he fashioned the shield, immense and strong,
richly adorned, and round its outer edge
he cast a triple rim, bright as the sun,
and from it hung a silver-bearing strap.
Fivefold the shield itself; and over it
the god, with all his wisdom, wrought a world.
There he made earth, and heaven, and sea,
the tireless sun, the moon at fullest light,
and all the signs that crown the face of heaven:
Pleiades and Hyades, Orion’s strength,
and the Bear, whom men also call the Wain,
who turns in place and watches great Orion,
alone unbathed by Ocean’s flowing stream.
Upon it too he made two cities fair,
filled with the speech and labor of mankind.
In one were marriages and marriage feasts:
by torchlight from their chambers brides were led
through streets alive with song; the wedding hymn
rose high, and young men whirled in dancing rings,
while flutes and lyres called clear beneath their hands.
Women stood wondering in the shadowed doors.
And in the marketplace a quarrel rose.
Two men contended over blood-price owed
for one slain dead. One cried that all was paid;
the other swore that he had taken nothing.
Both called for judgment, eager for an end.
The people shouted, favoring each in turn,
while heralds held them back. The elders sat
on polished stones within a sacred ring,
and in their hands they held the heralds’ staves.
Then each in turn rose up and gave his doom.
Between them lay two talents of pure gold,
a prize for him whose judgment proved most just.
Around the other city lay two hosts,
their armor glittering, bright in siege array.
Two counsels pleased them: either utterly
to sack the town, or share among themselves
all treasure that the lovely city held.
But those within would not submit or yield.
They armed for ambush. On the walls there stood
their wives, their little children, and the old,
keeping the city. Out the warriors went,
and Ares led them, with Athena’s might,
both wrought in gold, and golden were their robes,
tall, beautiful, and splendid in their arms,
as gods are; smaller were the men around.
They came where they had chosen ambuscade,
beside a river, watering-place of herds,
and there they hid themselves in shining bronze.
Apart from them two watchmen took their stand,
to spy the sheep and shambling cattle’s tread.
Soon came the flocks and cattle, and with them
two herdsmen piping, innocent of doom.
Then from their hiding-place the armed men sprang;
they seized the herds, cut off the white-fleeced sheep,
and struck the herdsmen down beside their beasts.
The besiegers, seated in their place of speech,
heard sudden tumult rising from the herds.
At once they mounted high-stepping horses,
pursued, and overtook them by the stream.
There, face to face, they fought with bronze-tipped spears.
And Strife was there, and Tumult, and dark Fate,
who held one newly wounded, one unhurt,
and dragged one dead man by the feet through dust.
Upon her shoulders hung a garment red
with human blood. They struggled, living-like,
and each side drew away the bodies of the slain.
Then he made a field, soft, rich, and broad,
three times ploughed over. Many ploughmen there
drove teams across it, turning to and fro.
And when a man had reached the field’s far edge
and wheeled his team, a servant came to him
and put into his hands a cup of wine,
honey-sweet; then again he took the furrow,
eager to reach the deep field’s farther side.
Behind them, though the soil was wrought of gold,
the land grew dark, as newly broken earth:
a marvel fashioned by the god’s own hand.
And there he made a king’s estate in harvest.
Reapers moved through the grain with sharpened hooks;
thick fell the handfuls down along the swath,
and binders gathered them in bands of straw.
Three binders stood nearby; behind them boys
collected armfuls of the fallen grain
and bore them on. The king, in silence, stood
beside the swath, staff in his hand, rejoicing.
Beneath an oak the heralds set a feast:
they dressed a great ox newly sacrificed,
while women scattered barley, white and bright,
to make the harvest-supper for the men.
He made a vineyard, heavy-clustered, fair,
golden and beautiful. The grapes hung dark;
the vines were propped on silver stakes. Around
he drew a ditch of blue, and round that ditch
a fence of tin. One pathway led within,
where gatherers passed in season of the vintage.
Girls and young men, light-hearted, carried fruit
in woven baskets. In their midst a boy
played sweetly on a clear-toned lyre and sang
a delicate song; the others followed him
with beating feet, with cries, and dancing joy.
He made a herd of cattle, straight of horn.
The cows were wrought of gold and tin; they lowed
as from the farmyard toward the pastureland
they hurried, by a murmuring river’s side
and waving reeds. Four golden herdsmen went
beside them, and nine quick-foot dogs behind.
But from the foremost herd two dreadful lions
had seized a bellowing bull and dragged him off.
Young men and dogs came running after them.
The lions tore the great hide, drank the blood,
and ate the entrails, while the herdsmen urged
their dogs in vain. The hounds shrank back from teeth;
they stood nearby and barked, but dared not bite.
Then the renowned lame god made pastureland,
a valley beautiful and wide, with sheep,
white flocks, and huts, and roofed folds, and pens.
And there he made a dancing-place, like one
which Daedalus in spacious Knossos wrought
for Ariadne of the lovely hair.
There boys and maidens, worth rich bridal gifts,
danced hand in hand, each holding by the wrist.
The maidens wore fine linen; the young men
wore tunics woven well and faintly gleaming,
soft with oil. The girls had lovely wreaths;
the men had golden knives from silver belts.
Now all together, with accomplished feet,
they ran in circles, as a potter tries
his wheel between his hands to see it run;
now back and forth they moved in facing lines.
A crowd stood round that longed-for dance, delighted.
Among them two skilled tumblers led the song
and whirled between the dancers as they sang.
And last, around the outer rim, he set
the mighty river Ocean, deep and strong.
Essential Questions Why does Homer go to such lengths to describe Hephaestus’ crafting of this shield? What does it mean that Hephaestus “wrought a world”? What does the shield, which Achilles is to carry into battle, depict? What sort of world(s) is depicted? What does this say about the world outside of war? Why give Achilles the world to carry with him into battle? What does this suggest to us about the power and purpose of art and representation? Advanced Questions Show Hide What can we say about the tension here between the act of creation in the context of war, destruction, and violence? What is the significance of the depiction of the quarrel in the marketplace? Can art be redemptive? Contrast with Auden’s ekphrasis (see below) Describe the world depicted in Auden’s shield. What is he saying regarding warfare, modern and Bronze Age? Vocabulary Ekphrasis — a passage in which words try to make an artwork vividly present to the reader, often by describing not only what the artwork looks like, but what it seems to mean, how it moves the viewer, or what story it contains Additional Poems and Texts The Shield of Achilles (1952)
W. H. Auden
She looked over his shoulder
For vines and olive trees,
Marble well-governed cities
And ships upon untamed seas,
But there on the shining metal
His hands had put instead
An artificial wilderness
And a sky like lead.
A plain without a feature, bare and brown,
No blade of grass, no sign of neighborhood,
Nothing to eat and nowhere to sit down,
Yet, congregated on its blankness, stood
An unintelligible multitude,
A million eyes, a million boots in line,
Without expression, waiting for a sign.
Out of the air a voice without a face
Proved by statistics that some cause was just
In tones as dry and level as the place:
No one was cheered and nothing was discussed;
Column by column in a cloud of dust
They marched away enduring a belief
Whose logic brought them, somewhere else, to grief.
She looked over his shoulder
For ritual pieties,
White flower-garlanded heifers,
Libation and sacrifice,
But there on the shining metal
Where the altar should have been,
She saw by his flickering forge-light
Quite another scene.
Barbed wire enclosed an arbitrary spot
Where bored officials lounged (one cracked a joke)
And sentries sweated for the day was hot:
A crowd of ordinary decent folk
Watched from without and neither moved nor spoke
As three pale figures were led forth and bound
To three posts driven upright in the ground.
The mass and majesty of this world, all
That carries weight and always weighs the same
Lay in the hands of others; they were small
And could not hope for help and no help came:
What their foes liked to do was done, their shame
Was all the worst could wish; they lost their pride
And died as men before their bodies died.
She looked over his shoulder
For athletes at their games,
Men and women in a dance
Moving their sweet limbs
Quick, quick, to music,
But there on the shining shield
His hands had set no dancing-floor
But a weed-choked field.
A ragged urchin, aimless and alone,
Loitered about that vacancy; a bird
Flew up to safety from his well-aimed stone:
That girls are raped, that two boys knife a third,
Were axioms to him, who’d never heard
Of any world where promises were kept,
Or one could weep because another wept.
The thin-lipped armorer,
Hephaestos, hobbled away,
Thetis of the shining breasts
Cried out in dismay
At what the god had wrought
To please her son, the strong
Iron-hearted man-slaying Achilles
Who would not live long.
Teacher notes Show Hide Auden — negative or revisionary ekphrasis Notes on the poetic structure of Auden’s The Shield of Achilles: Notice the very deliberate use of meter, structure and form We start with (implied) Thetis looking over Hephaestus’ shoulder She has certain expectations of what should be depicted on such a shield: rites, ways of life, harmony, sacrifice, harvest, fertility, dancing, games, etc These stanzas are in a loosely-ballad form which sounds simpler, older, song-like, ancient, resonant, folksy, natural But what does she see instead? She see a moral desert, soldiers in line, violence, execution, barbed wire, bureaucracy, emptiness And notice these stanzas are in an entirely different form They are longer, descriptive, and in “Rhyme Royal”: with the pattern: ababbcc associated with Chaucer more discursive and philosophical and strikes with a particularly pitiless “cc” at the end of each stanza i.e.:
Expectation: She looked over his shoulder
For ritual pieties,
White flower-garlanded heifers,
Libation and sacrifice
Reality:
As three pale figures were led forth and bound
To three posts driven upright in the ground.
So for further exploration and analysis: How does Auden use the very forms of the poem to reinforce his meaning? And, never to lose track of: what is the meaning?

title: Ekphrasis II
content:
Venus, Mother of Aeneas, Presenting him with Arms Forged by Vulcan by Nicolas Poussin (1635) The Shield of Aeneas
Virgil, Aeneid 8.626–731
But Venus, bright among the clouds of heaven,
came bearing gifts; and when, in secret vale,
she saw her son apart by cooling stream,
she stood before him, radiant, and she spoke:
“Behold the promised gifts, my son, fulfilled
by Vulcan’s art. Now do not fear the proud
Laurentines, nor the threats of Turnus’ war.”
She said, and sought her child’s embrace, and laid
the glittering arms beneath an oak before him.
Aeneas gazed, rejoicing in the gifts,
the terrible honor of the god’s own hand.
He could not have enough of them: he turned
his eyes from piece to piece; he wondered, touched,
and lifted in his hands the crested helm,
the sword that breathed out death, the stiff bronze mail,
blood-red and vast, like some dark thundercloud
that burns beneath the sun and flashes fire;
the polished greaves of electrum and gold,
the spear, and then the shield, beyond all words.
There had the lord of fire, who knew the fates,
who knew the age to come, engraved the tale
of Italy, the triumphs of the Romans,
the whole long lineage of Ascanius’ seed,
and all the wars they fought, in order shown.
There too he made the mother wolf, stretched out
within the green cave sacred to Mars’ name;
around her teats the twin boys hung and played,
fearless beneath her, sucking at the beast,
while she bent back her neck and licked each child,
and shaped their bodies gently with her tongue.
Not far from these he set the walls of Rome,
and Sabine women seized from crowded seats
when the great games were held; then sudden war
between the sons of Romulus and old
Tatius, stern king of Cures. Soon the kings,
their strife laid down, stood armed before Jove’s shrine,
holding their cups, and struck a treaty there,
above the slain sow’s body.
Near this, the four-horse chariots tore apart
false Mettus, traitor—Alba, you should have
kept faith. Tullus dragged through the woods the limbs
of him who lied; the bloody brambles dripped.
There Porsenna ordered Rome to take again
her banished Tarquin, and with mighty siege
pressed on the city. Rome’s sons rushed to arms
for freedom. He stood like one enraged, because
Cocles had dared to break the bridge, because
Cloelia, snapping bonds, had crossed the stream.
Upon the height Manlius, guardian of the fort,
stood firm before the temple, holding Rome;
the palace bristled fresh with Romulus’ thatch.
And there, through gilded colonnades, the goose
of silver cried that Gauls were at the gate.
The Gauls moved through the thickets, near the fort,
protected by the darkness and the gift
of shadowy night. Their hair was golden; gold
shone on their cloaks; their striped bright mantles blazed;
their milk-white necks were circled round with gold.
Each brandished two Alpine spears; their long shields
covered their bodies.
Here he had wrought the dancing Salii,
the naked Luperci, wool-bound sacred caps,
and shields that fell from heaven. Chaste mothers rode
in cushioned cars through Rome to solemn rites.
Far off from these, he added Tartarus,
the deep abodes of Dis, the penalties
of crime; and you, Catiline, hung there,
trembling before the Furies’ faces. There
the righteous stood apart, and Cato gave
the dead their laws.
Around these images the sea was poured,
swelling in gold, though hoary foam was white
upon the blue-gray waves; and dolphins bright
with silver swept in circles with their tails
and cleft the flood.
At center: bronze fleets, the Actian war,
Leucate all alive with ordered ships,
and all the waves made golden. Caesar stood
upon the high stern, leading Italy,
the fathers, people, household gods, and great
Penates; from his radiant temples streamed
his father’s star. Elsewhere, with favoring winds
and gods, Agrippa led his towering line;
his brow was bright with naval crown, whose beaks
rose proud, the splendid token of the sea.
Against them, Antony with barbarous wealth
and motley arms, victorious from the East
and crimson shores, brought Egypt, eastern might,
and farthest Bactra; and behind him came—
shame of it—his Egyptian wife.
All rushed together. All the sea was torn,
convulsed by oars, by triple-pointed prows.
They drove for open water. You would think
the Cyclades, uprooted, swam the deep,
or mountains clashed with mountains, such the weight
with which the men pressed on from towered ships.
Flame, tow, and flying steel were hurled by hand;
Neptune’s blue fields grew red with slaughtered men.
The queen amid them called her ships with sistrum,
not yet turning to look at twin snakes near.
Monstrous gods of every shape, and barking
Anubis, raised their weapons against Neptune,
Venus, and Minerva. In the midst,
Mars raged in iron; from the heavens grim
Furies flew; Discord walked with torn robe,
delighted, and Bellona followed her
with bloody whip.
Apollo, watching from Actium’s height,
bent his bow. At that terror, Egypt turned,
and India, Arab, Saba, all took flight.
The queen herself seemed calling winds to aid,
loosening her sails, already pale with death.
The fire-god made her driven by the waves
and western wind through carnage; opposite,
the Nile, in sorrow, opened wide his folds and summoned conquered peoples to his breast,
his sheltering blue.
But Caesar, borne in triple triumph home
through Roman walls, dedicated to the gods
immortal vows: three hundred shrines throughout
the city. Streets rang out with joy and games
and clapping hands. In every temple stood
a choir of mothers; altars in each shrine;
before the altars slaughtered bullocks lay.
Caesar himself, before bright Phoebus’ doors,
sat and reviewed the gifts of conquered lands,
then hung them on the splendid posts. The tribes
of vanquished nations passed in long array,
diverse in dress, in arms, in speech, in mode.
Here Vulcan shaped the Nomads, and the loose-
robed Africans; here Leleges, Carians,
Geloni bearing arrows. Euphrates went
with humbled waves; Morini, farthest men;
the two-horned Rhine; Dahae unsubdued;
and Araxes, indignant at his bridge.
Such scenes he wondered at upon the shield,
his mother’s gift, the fire-god’s unknown tale.
He did not know the things themselves, but joyed
to see their images; and on his shoulder
lifted the fame and fate of sons to come.
The New Colossus
Emma Lazarus
Written in 1883 for the Art Loan Fund Exhibition in Aid of the Bartholdi Pedestal Fund for the Statue of Liberty. Public domain.
Not like the brazen giant of Greek fame,
With conquering limbs astride from land to land;
Here at our sea-washed, sunset gates shall stand
A mighty woman with a torch, whose flame
Is the imprisoned lightning, and her name
Mother of Exiles. From her beacon-hand
Glows world-wide welcome; her mild eyes command
The air-bridged harbor that twin cities frame.
“Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!” cries she
With silent lips. “Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,
The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.
Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door!”
The Old Colossus and the New Lazarus constructs her national ideal through a deliberate contrast between two monumental figures. The ancient Colossus appears as an emblem of conquest, bestriding a harbour with weapons and flame. The “new colossus” preserves the immense scale and the torch but transforms their meaning: power becomes protection, and the harbour becomes an entrance for exiles rather than a boundary defended against them.
The Old Colossus and the New 1 / 1
Philips Galle, after Maarten van Heemskerck, The Colossus of Rhodes, from The Eight Wonders of the World, 1572. Hand-coloured engraving. Bronze plaque bearing Emma Lazarus’s “The New Colossus,” installed within the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty in 1903. PREVIOUS NEXT Essential Questions Recalling previous unit’s passage — Homer describing the forging of Achilles’ shield — what are the similarities and differences we can identify in this passage? Is Virgil doing something different with the picture he paints? What is his purpose? Is this passage myth-making, is it prophecy, is it propaganda? What is the significance of Aeneas carrying this particular object into battle with him? Advanced Questions Show Hide Which shield — Achilles’ or Aeneas’, Homer’s or Virgil’s — depicts a whole World, and which depicts the particular? Is one more idealogical than the other? How does Virgil’s passage regard violence and war as compared to Homer’s? Why might Virgil desire to absorb this particular bit of what is essentially Ancient Greece’s origin mythology into that of Rome? How does this passage regard rites and sacrifices? What can we say about Aeneas not recognizing or understanding what he sees depicted on the shield? Vocabulary Epic — a long narrative poem concerned with heroic action, divine forces, and communal destiny Teleology — the interpretation of events as moving toward a predetermined end or purpose Propaganda — communication designed to shape public belief or feeling in the service of a political, religious, or ideological cause. It does not have to be false; it often works by selecting, arranging, beautifying, simplifying, or emotionally charging facts so that the audience sees one interpretation as natural, noble, or necessary Dactylic hexameter — the classical epic meter used by Homer and Virgil. Each line has six metrical feet, built mainly from dactyls — long-short-short — and spondees — long-long. In Latin, the meter is based on syllable length, not stress accent. Teacher notes Show Hide Notice that the images of the shield occupy time as well as space Notice that the history told is not merely triumphal. The whole sweep of Roman formation is there, with all its violence and all its burden. Think of the intended reader of this ekphrasis, a Roman knowing and recognizing the future which Aeneas carries with him but does not yet know himself. Recall Homer’s emphasis on personal and social life. Rites, dancing, rituals, games. Here the images describe are national.

title: Ekphrasis III
content:
Image Gallery 1 / 1
Tracing of an engraving of the Sosibios vase by Keats. The Sosibios Vase is a Neo-Attic marble krater of the Hellenistic period. It is attributed by signature to Sosibios, a Greek sculptor who was active in Rome during the end of the Roman Republic, and is dated to approximately 50 BC. It is Sosibios’ only known work. PREVIOUS NEXT Ode on a Grecian Urn (1819)
John Keats
Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness,
Thou foster-child of silence and slow time,
Sylvan historian, who canst thus express
A flowery tale more sweetly than our rhyme:
What leaf-fring’d legend haunts about thy shape
Of deities or mortals, or of both,
In Tempe or the dales of Arcady?
What men or gods are these? What maidens loth?
What mad pursuit? What struggle to escape?
What pipes and timbrels? What wild ecstasy?
Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard
Are sweeter; therefore, ye soft pipes, play on;
Not to the sensual ear, but, more endear’d,
Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone:
Fair youth, beneath the trees, thou canst not leave
Thy song, nor ever can those trees be bare;
Bold Lover, never, never canst thou kiss,
Though winning near the goal yet, do not grieve;
She cannot fade, though thou hast not thy bliss,
For ever wilt thou love, and she be fair!
Ah, happy, happy boughs! that cannot shed
Your leaves, nor ever bid the Spring adieu;
And, happy melodist, unwearied,
For ever piping songs for ever new;
More happy love! more happy, happy love!
For ever warm and still to be enjoy’d,
For ever panting, and for ever young;
All breathing human passion far above,
That leaves a heart high-sorrowful and cloy’d,
A burning forehead, and a parching tongue.
Who are these coming to the sacrifice?
To what green altar, O mysterious priest,
Lead’st thou that heifer lowing at the skies,
And all her silken flanks with garlands drest?
What little town by river or sea shore,
Or mountain-built with peaceful citadel,
Is emptied of this folk, this pious morn?
And, little town, thy streets for evermore
Will silent be; and not a soul to tell
Why thou art desolate, can e’er return.
O Attic shape! Fair attitude! with brede
Of marble men and maidens overwrought,
With forest branches and the trodden weed;
Thou, silent form, dost tease us out of thought
As doth eternity: Cold Pastoral!
When old age shall this generation waste,
Thou shalt remain, in midst of other woe
Than ours, a friend to man, to whom thou say’st,
“Beauty is truth, truth beauty,—that is all
Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.”
The Miletus torso (c. 480–470 BC) at the Louvre has been suggested as Rilke’s subject. Archaic Torso of Apollo (1908)
Rainer Maria Rilke
We cannot know his legendary head
with eyes like ripening fruit. And yet his torso
is still suffused with brilliance from inside,
like a lamp, in which his gaze, now turned to low,
gleams in all its power. Otherwise
the curved breast could not dazzle you so, nor could
a smile run through the placid hips and thighs
to that dark center where procreation flared.
Otherwise this stone would seem defaced
beneath the translucent cascade of the shoulders
and would not glisten like a wild beast’s fur:
would not, from all the borders of itself,
burst like a star: for here there is no place
that does not see you. You must change your life.
Essential Questions Who or what is Keats addressing? Notice “Thou” Why slow time? “A flowery tale more sweetly than our rhyme”; Can images speak more than words? What about the paradox that this is itself written in a poem? Who or what is Rilke addressing? What could it possibly mean to say ‘Beauty is Truth, Truth Beauty’? What does Rilke say makes this fragment or ruin still powerful? What is the Volta in Rilke’s Archaic Torso of Apollo? How is it that contemplating a fragment of ancient art could compel such a lightning bolt? Advanced Questions Show Hide How do these examples of ekphrasis differ from the ancient examples of the previous units? Is there some way in which a fragment or a partial ruin could be more powerful than the whole? Is the urn — a work of art — greater or lesser than lived, mortal life in its permanence, stillness? Vocabulary Lyric poem — a short or concentrated poem focused on a speaker’s feeling, thought, or experience Ode — a lyric poem that addresses, praises, reflects on, or meditates upon a person, object, idea, place, or experience Sonnet — a 14-line lyric poem that develops one central idea or feeling and usually includes a volta, or turn in thought Volta — the “turn” in a sonnet, where the poem shifts in thought, feeling, argument, or address Epiphany — a moment of revelation Imperative — a command form: “You must…” Apostrophe — directly addressing someone or something absent, dead, or unable to answer. Teacher notes Show Hide Notice the double meaning of “still”: “Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness” Notice that both works are full of mystery. Keats asks many unanswered questions of the urn’s images, and it is essential that Rilke describes a partial ruin. “Maidens loth” suggests reluctance. It is not all Arkady pastoral idyll. The erotic, and even violence, looms. Notice the repetition: “Bold Lover, never, never canst thou kiss”. Keats first suggests that there may be something beautiful in trees which can never be bare, but then what of the lover whose pursuit will “never, never” attain his beloved? In stanza 4, Keats no imagines what cannot be seen, the town left behind by the pious procession; a town that will forever be empty. What does “as doth eternity” mean? “Cold Pastoral!” And of course: what is the final couplet doing? Beauty is truth? Truth, beauty? That’s all ye need to know? Who is saying this? Keats? The urn? Does anybody mean it? Notice the use of form. Keats’ stanzas start with a Shakespearean quatrain, with a simple rhyming scheme. But then these are following by less formulaic and more varied sestets; almost as if the speaker starts out sure of something, but becomes less so. Keats contemplates the stillness of a work of art, Rilke is stunned by how alive, forceful, even fecund a headless old torso can be. Apollo’s torso even radiates beyond its borders, and shimmers like the skin of a wild beast or predator. Apollo moves from being blind, to being all-seeing. Compare the erotic in each. Compare absence in each. Remember that Rilke is originally German. Printed above is perhaps the most accessible. But it may lack some of the original German’s strangeness and compactness. See the filling 1957 translation by C.F. MacIntyre: Never will we know his fabulous head
where the eyes’ apples slowly ripened. Yet
his torso glows: a candelabrum set
before his gaze which is pushed back and hid,
restrained and shining. Else the curving breast
could not thus blind you, nor through the soft turn
of the loins could this smile easily have passed
into the bright groins where the genitals burned.
Else stood this stone a fragment and defaced,
with lucent body from the shoulders falling,
too short, not gleaming like a lion’s fell;
nor would this star have shaken the shackles off,
bursting with light, until there is no place
that does not see you. You must change your life.

title: Elegy and Memory
summary: Catullus and the language of mourning
content:
Unit plan
Purpose. The unit introduces apostrophe, ritual address, remembrance, and the limitations of memorial art.
Visual plan. A two-work comparison between private familial remembrance and public civic memorial.
Artworks and Images Greek Funerary Memorials 1 / 1
Grave Stele of Hegeso, c. 410–400 BCE. Marble relief. Photograph by George E. Koronaios, CC BY-SA 4.0. Grave Stele of Dexileos, 394–393 BCE. Marble relief. Photograph by George E. Koronaios, CC BY-SA 4.0. PREVIOUS NEXT Looking at the Images The two stelai use the same funerary medium for very different kinds of remembrance:
Hegeso is shown in an enclosed domestic scene, selecting jewelry with an attendant; quiet gestures of interrupted ordinary life. Dexileos appears mounted above a stricken enemy, a public image of courage and civic identity. Featured Poems and Texts Catullus 101
Catullus
Translated by Robinson Ellis (1871)
Borne o’er many a land, o’er many a level of ocean,
Here to the grave I come, brother, of holy repose,
Sadly the last poor gifts, death’s simple duty, to bring thee;
Unto the silent dust vainly to murmur a cry.
Since thy form deep-shrouded an evil destiny taketh
From me, O hapless ghost, brother, O heavily ta’en,
Yet this bounty the while, these gifts ancestral of usance
Homely, the sad slight store piety grants to the tomb;
Drench’d in a brother’s tears, and weeping freshly, receive them;
Yea, take, brother, a long Ave, a timeless adieu.
Heraclitus
Callimachus
Translated by William Johnson Cory
They told me, Heraclitus, they told me you were dead,
They brought me bitter news to hear and bitter tears to shed.
I wept, as I remembered, how often you and I
Had tired the sun with talking and sent him down the sky.
And now that thou art lying, my dear old Carian guest,
A handful of grey ashes, long, long ago at rest,
Still are thy pleasant voices, thy nightingales, awake;
For Death, he taketh all away, but them he cannot take.

These three funerary epigrams move from the public language of the city to increasingly personal forms of remembrance:

Philip the father laid here
the twelve-years-old child,
his high hope, Nicoteles. Crethis Unlike the public heroism of the first epigram or the concentrated parental grief of the second, this poem remembers Crethis through the ordinary qualities that made her irreplaceable: her stories, games, conversation, and companionship:

PREVIOUS NEXT Looking at the Images Move through this sequence spatially. Autun’s tympanum places judgment above the church entrance; Chartres then expands the sculptural threshold into a complete architectural environment of portals, vertical ascent, colored light, and processional movement. The pilgrim badge reduces a great shrine to a small object that could be worn and carried home.
Botticelli’s diagram does for Dante’s imagined afterworld what a cathedral plan does for a building: it turns a difficult journey into organized space. Ask how each visual system directs movement and assigns meaning to location.
Featured Poems and Texts The Gate and the Crossing Dante and his guide, the Roman poet Virgil, have reached the entrance to Hell. The canto moves through a sequence of morally charged spaces: the inscribed gate, the dark vestibule occupied by those who refused both good and evil, and the shore of Acheron, where Charon gathers the dead. Dante’s journey turns spiritual judgment into architecture, geography, and directed movement.
Inferno, Canto III
Dante Alighieri
Translated from the Italian by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1867). Public-domain text.
“Through me the way is to the city dolent;
Through me the way is to eternal dole;
Through me the way among the people lost.
Justice incited my sublime Creator;
Created me divine Omnipotence,
The highest Wisdom and the primal Love.
Before me there were no created things,
Only eterne, and I eternal last.
All hope abandon, ye who enter in!”
These words in sombre colour I beheld
Written upon the summit of a gate;
Whence I: “Their sense is, Master, hard to me!”
And he to me, as one experienced:
“Here all suspicion needs must be abandoned,
All cowardice must needs be here extinct.
We to the place have come, where I have told thee
Thou shalt behold the people dolorous
Who have foregone the good of intellect.”
And after he had laid his hand on mine
With joyful mien, whence I was comforted,
He led me in among the secret things.
There sighs, complaints, and ululations loud
Resounded through the air without a star,
Whence I, at the beginning, wept thereat.
Languages diverse, horrible dialects,
Accents of anger, words of agony,
And voices high and hoarse, with sound of hands,
Made up a tumult that goes whirling on
For ever in that air for ever black,
Even as the sand doth, when the whirlwind breathes.
And I, who had my head with horror bound,
Said: “Master, what is this which now I hear?
What folk is this, which seems by pain so vanquished?”
And he to me: “This miserable mode
Maintain the melancholy souls of those
Who lived withouten infamy or praise.
Commingled are they with that caitiff choir
Of Angels, who have not rebellious been,
Nor faithful were to God, but were for self.
The heavens expelled them, not to be less fair;
Nor them the nethermore abyss receives,
For glory none the damned would have from them.”
And I: “O Master, what so grievous is
To these, that maketh them lament so sore?”
He answered: “I will tell thee very briefly.
These have no longer any hope of death;
And this blind life of theirs is so debased,
They envious are of every other fate.
No fame of them the world permits to be;
Misericord and Justice both disdain them.
Let us not speak of them, but look, and pass.”
And I, who looked again, beheld a banner,
Which, whirling round, ran on so rapidly,
That of all pause it seemed to me indignant;
And after it there came so long a train
Of people, that I ne’er would have believed
That ever Death so many had undone.
When some among them I had recognised,
I looked, and I beheld the shade of him
Who made through cowardice the great refusal.
Forthwith I comprehended, and was certain,
That this the sect was of the caitiff wretches
Hateful to God and to his enemies.
These miscreants, who never were alive,
Were naked, and were stung exceedingly
By gadflies and by hornets that were there.
These did their faces irrigate with blood,
Which, with their tears commingled, at their feet
By the disgusting worms was gathered up.
And when to gazing farther I betook me,
People I saw on a great river’s bank;
Whence said I: “Master, now vouchsafe to me,
That I may know who these are, and what law
Makes them appear so ready to pass over,
As I discern athwart the dusky light.”
And he to me: “These things shall all be known
To thee, as soon as we our footsteps stay
Upon the dismal shore of Acheron.”
Then with mine eyes ashamed and downward cast,
Fearing my words might irksome be to him,
From speech refrained I till we reached the river.
And lo! towards us coming in a boat
An old man, hoary with the hair of eld,
Crying: “Woe unto you, ye souls depraved!
Hope nevermore to look upon the heavens;
I come to lead you to the other shore,
To the eternal shades in heat and frost.
And thou, that yonder standest, living soul,
Withdraw thee from these people, who are dead!”
But when he saw that I did not withdraw,
He said: “By other ways, by other ports
Thou to the shore shalt come, not here, for passage;
A lighter vessel needs must carry thee.”
And unto him the Guide: “Vex thee not, Charon;
It is so willed there where is power to do
That which is willed; and farther question not.”
Thereat were quieted the fleecy cheeks
Of him the ferryman of the livid fen,
Who round about his eyes had wheels of flame.
But all those souls who weary were and naked
Their colour changed and gnashed their teeth together,
As soon as they had heard those cruel words.
God they blasphemed and their progenitors,
The human race, the place, the time, the seed
Of their engendering and of their birth!
Thereafter all together they drew back,
Bitterly weeping, to the accursed shore,
Which waiteth every man who fears not God.
Charon the demon, with the eyes of glede,
Beckoning to them, collects them all together,
Beats with his oar whoever lags behind.
As in the autumn-time the leaves fall off,
First one and then another, till the branch
Unto the earth surrenders all its spoils;
In similar wise the evil seed of Adam
Throw themselves from that margin one by one,
At signals, as a bird unto its lure.
So they depart across the dusky wave,
And ere upon the other side they land,
Again on this side a new troop assembles.
“My son,” the courteous Master said to me,
“All those who perish in the wrath of God
Here meet together out of every land;
And ready are they to pass o’er the river,
Because celestial Justice spurs them on,
So that their fear is turned into desire.
This way there never passes a good soul;
And hence if Charon doth complain of thee,
Well mayst thou know now what his speech imports.”
This being finished, all the dusk champaign
Trembled so violently, that of that terror
The recollection bathes me still with sweat.
The land of tears gave forth a blast of wind,
And fulminated a vermilion light,
Which overmastered in me every sense,
And as a man whom sleep hath seized I fell.
The Pilgrims Gather and the Tale-Telling Game As spring returns, travellers from across England set out for the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury. At the Tabard Inn in Southwark, Chaucer joins a company drawn from different occupations, ranks, and ways of life. The road becomes both a religious pilgrimage and a temporary social world: the travellers reveal themselves through their clothing, conduct, conversation, and eventually the stories they tell.
This selection introduces the company, then contrasts the Knight’s chivalric ideal, the Wife of Bath’s worldly experience, and the Pardoner’s exploitation of religious belief. It concludes with the Host transforming the journey into an organized tale-telling contest.
The Canterbury Tales: General Prologue
Geoffrey Chaucer
Selected passages from the General Prologue; modern English version by A. S. Kline. Reproduced for non-commercial educational use.
When that April with his showers sweet
The drought of March has pierced root deep,
And bathed each vein with liquor of such power
That engendered from it is the flower,
When Zephyrus too with his gentle strife,
To every field and wood, has brought new life
In tender shoots, and the youthful sun
Half his course through the Ram has run,
And little birds are making melody,
Who all the night with open eye do sleep –
Nature their hearts in every way so pricks –
Then people long to go on pilgrimage,
And palmers who seek out foreign strands,
To far-off shrines, renowned in sundry lands;
And specially, from every shire’s end
Of England, down to Canterbury they wend,
The holy blissful martyr there to seek,
Who had aided them when they were sick.
It befell that in that season on a day,
In Southwark at The Tabard as I lay,
Ready to set out on my pilgrimage
To Canterbury with pious courage,
There came at night to that hostelry
Quite nine and twenty in a company
Of sundry folk who had chanced to fall
Into a fellowship, and pilgrims all,
That towards Canterbury meant to ride.
The chambers and the stables were full wide,
And we housed at our ease, and of the best;
And shortly, when the sun had gone to rest,
I had such speech with each and everyone,
That of their fellowship I soon made one,
Agreeing I would make an early rise,
To take our way there, as I now advise.
Nonetheless while I have time and space,
Before a step more of my tale I pace,
It seems to me in full accord with reason,
To tell you everything of their condition,
Of each of them, as they appeared to me,
And who they were, and of what degree,
And what apparel they were travelling in;
And with a knight then I will first begin.
There was a KNIGHT and he a worthy man,
That from the day on which he first began,
To ride abroad, had followed chivalry,
Truth, honour, courtesy and charity.
He had fought nobly in his lord’s war,
And ridden to the fray, and no man more,
As much in Christendom as heathen place,
And ever honoured for his worth and grace.
When we took Alexandria was there;
Often at table held the place of honour,
Above all other nations too in Prussia;
Campaigned in Lithuania and Russia,
No Christian man of his rank more often.
At the siege of Algeciras had he been,
In Granada, and on Moroccan shore;
He was at Ayash and Antalya
When taken, and many times had been
In action on the Mediterranean Sea.
Of mortal battles he had seen fifteen,
And fought for the faith at Tramissene
Thrice in the lists and always slain his foe.
This same worthy knight had been also
With the Emir of Balat once, at work
With him against some other heathen Turk;
Won him a reputation highly prized,
And though he was valiant, he was wise,
And in his manner modest as a maid.
And never a discourtesy he said
In all his life to those who met his sight;
He was a very perfect gentle knight.
But to tell of his equipment, his array,
His horses fine, he wore no colours gay,
Sported a tunic, padded fustian
On which his coat of mail left many a stain;
For he was scarcely back from his voyage,
And going now to make his pilgrimage.
Chaucer next describes other members of the company before turning to the Wife of Bath.
A good WIFE was there from next to BATH,
But pity was that she was somewhat deaf.
In cloth-making she was excellent,
Surpassing those of Ypres and of Ghent.
In all the parish there was no wife, so
Before her to the Offertory might go –
And if they did, indeed, so angry she
That she was quite put out of charity.
Her kerchiefs were finely wove I found;
I dare to swear those weighed a good ten pounds,
That on a Sunday she wore on her head.
Her hose were of a fine scarlet red,
And tightly tied: her shoes full soft and new.
Bold was her face, and fair and red of hue.
Had been a worthy woman all her life;
Husbands at the church-door she had five,
Besides other company in her youth –
No need to speak of that just now, in truth.
And thrice had she been to Jerusalem;
She had crossed many a foreign stream.
At Boulogne she had been, and Rome,
St James of Compostella, and Cologne,
And she knew much of wandering by the way.
Gap-toothed was she, truthfully to say.
At ease upon a saddle-horse she sat,
Well wimpled, and on her head a hat
As wide as a small buckler or large shield,
Her large hips an over-skirt concealed,
And on her feet a pair of sharp spurs sat.
In fellowship she loved to laugh and chat;
And remedies for love she had, by chance,
For in that art she knew the oldest dance.
After several further portraits, Chaucer introduces the Pardoner, a church official who sells indulgences and supposed relics.
With him there rode a noble PARDONER
Of Charing Cross, his friend and his peer,
Returned directly from the Court of Rome.
He sang out loud: ‘Come hither, love, to me!’
The Summoner sang a powerful bass around;
Never a trumpet of half so great a sound.
The Pardoner had hair as yellow as wax,
But smooth it hung like a hank of flax.
In clusters hung the locks he possessed,
With which his shoulders he overspread;
But thin they fell, in strands, one by one.
But hood, to adorn them, he wore none,
For it was trussed up in his wallet –
He thought he rode fashionably set;
Dishevelled, save his cap, he rode all bare.
Such bulging eyeballs had he as a hare.
A pilgrim badge had he sewn on his cap;
His wallet lay before him in his lap,
Brimful of pardons, come from Rome hotfoot.
A voice he had as small as has a goat;
No beard had he, nor ever looked to have;
As smooth it were as it were lately shaved –
I judge he was a gelding or a mare.
But of his craft, from Berwick unto Ware,
Never was such another Pardoner.
And in his bag a pillow-case was there,
Which he claimed was Our Lady’s veil;
He said he had a fragment of the sail
That Saint Peter used, when he skimmed
Upon the sea till Jesus summoned him.
He had a cross of brass set with stones,
And in a glass, he had pigs’ bones.
And with these relics, when he had to hand
Some poor parson living on the land,
In one day he gathered in more money
Than the parson in a month of Sundays.
And thus with feigned flattery, his japes
Made people and the parson his apes.
But to tell true from first to last,
He was in church a noble ecclesiast.
He read a lesson well or a story,
But best of all he sang an Offertory.
For well he knew, when that song was sung,
He must preach and well tune his tongue
To win silver, as he well knew how;
Therefore he sang more sweetly and loud.
Having completed his portraits of the pilgrims, Chaucer returns to the evening at the Tabard Inn, where the Host proposes a tale-telling contest for the journey.
Our HOST made great cheer for everyone,
And down to supper set us all anon.
He served us with victuals of the best:
Strong was the wine, we drank with zest.
A handsome man our Host was withal,
And fit to be a marshal in a hall.
A large man he was with striking eyes;
No fairer burgess was there in Cheapside.
Bold in his speech, and wise, and well taught,
And of honest manhood he lacked naught.
Add that he was a truly merry man;
And after supper jokingly began
To speak of entertainment and other things,
After we had paid our reckonings,
Saying to us: ‘Now lordings, truly
To me you are right welcome, heartily!
For by my troth and telling you no lie,
I have not seen this year such folk go by
As gathered together in this tavern now.
And I would entertain, if I knew how,
Yet there is an entertainment, in my thoughts,
To amuse you and it will cost you naught.
You go to Canterbury – God you speed!
May the blissful martyr bless you indeed! –
And well I know, as you go on your way
You intend to chatter and make hay.
For truly, comfort and delight is none
In riding on the way dumb as a stone.
And therefore I offer you some sport,
As I first said, to give you some comfort.
And if you agree as one and consent
Each of you to accept my judgement,
And to work it as I to you will say,
Tomorrow when you ride on your way,
Now, by my father’s soul, he being dead,
If you lack merriment, be it on my head!
Hold up your hands, without longer speech.’
Our decision was not long to seek:
We thought it not worth serious debating,
And gave him leave, without deliberating,
And bade him give his orders as he wished.
‘Lordings,’ quoth he, ‘now listen to the rest –
But hear me out, I pray, without disdain –
Here is the point, to tell you short and plain:
That each of you, to speed you on your way,
On the journey there, shall tell two tales,
Till Canterbury, I mean it so,
And on the homeward way another two,
Of adventures that did once befall.
And which of you that bears them best of all –
That is to say, who tells in this case
Tales the most serious that most solace –
Shall have a supper and we pay the cost,
Here in this place, sitting by this post,
When that we come again from Canterbury.
And to make you all the more merry,
I will myself gladly with you ride,
All at my own cost, and be your guide.
And whoever my judgement does gainsay
Shall pay all that we spend by the way.
And if you will agree it shall be so,
Tell me now, without more ado,
And I will get me ready for the dawn.’
The thing was agreed, and our oath sworn
With right good heart, and we begged also
That he accordingly would do so,
And that he act then as our governor,
And of our tales be judge and recorder,
And fix the supper at a certain price,
And we would be ruled by his device,
In high and low, and thus by one assent
We all agreed to his true judgement.

title: High Renaissance to Mannerism
content:
Unit plan
Purpose. Students first see Renaissance pictorial order established and then watch that order strain, lengthen, twist, and become deliberately artificial.
Visual plan. A six-image transition gallery. Uccello establishes constructed pictorial order; Raphael gives its mature ideal; Michelangelo places that ideal under pressure; Pontormo, Parmigianino, and Bronzino make distortion and artificiality unmistakable.
Artworks and Images From Renaissance Order to Mannerist Distortion 1 / 1
Paolo Uccello, The Battle of San Romano (London panel), c. 1438–1440. Raphael, The School of Athens, 1509–1511. Michelangelo, The Last Judgment, 1536–1541. Pontormo, The Deposition, 1525–1528. Parmigianino, Madonna of the Long Neck, 1534–1540. Bronzino, An Allegory with Venus and Cupid, c. 1545. PREVIOUS NEXT Gethsemane: Mantegna and El Greco 1 / 1
Andrea Mantegna, The Agony in the Garden, about 1455–1456, egg tempera on wood, National Gallery, London. El Greco, The Agony in the Garden, about 1590–1595, oil on canvas, Toledo Museum of Art. PREVIOUS NEXT Looking at the Images Begin with Uccello’s conspicuous construction of pictorial space: fallen lances and shortened bodies make perspective itself part of the subject. Raphael converts that experiment into a spacious, balanced intellectual world. Michelangelo’s Last Judgment then overwhelms stable architecture with a rotating mass of bodies.
In Pontormo, Parmigianino, and Bronzino, elongation, improbable balance, compressed space, cold or heightened color, and ambiguous emotion are no longer failures to imitate nature. They are deliberate refinements of style. The gallery should make Mannerism visible as a transformation of Renaissance mastery, not merely as “bad proportion.”
Featured Poems and Texts On the Painting of the Sistine Chapel
Michelangelo Buonarroti
Translated by John Addington Symonds
I’ve grown a goitre by dwelling in this den—
As cats from stagnant streams in Lombardy,
Or in what other land they hap to be—
Which drives the belly close beneath the chin:
My beard turns up to heaven; my nape falls in,
Fixed on my spine: my breast-bone visibly
Grows like a harp: a rich embroidery
Bedews my face from brush-drops thick and thin.
My loins into my paunch like levers grind:
My buttock like a crupper bears my weight;
My feet unguided wander to and fro;
In front my skin grows loose and long; behind,
By bending it becomes more taut and strait;
Crosswise I strain me like a Syrian bow:
Whence false and quaint, I know,
Must be the fruit of squinting brain and eye;
For ill can aim the gun that bends awry.
Come then, Giovanni, try
To succour my dead pictures and my fame;
Since foul I fare and painting is my shame. Essential Questions Advanced Questions Show Hide Vocabulary Additional Poems and Texts Giorgio Vasari, a short passage on artistic style. John Donne, “The Flea,” as an optional literary analogy. Teacher notes Show Hide

title: Impressionism and Pointillism
content:
Unit plan
Purpose. Impressionism treats perception as fleeting and situated; Pointillism attempts to organize that fleeting perception through optical theory and method.
Visual plan. A five-part transition from atmospheric impression and modern social scenes to Seurat’s systematic reconstruction of sensation.
Artworks and Images From Impression to Optical System 1 / 1
Claude Monet, Impression, Sunrise, 1872. Berthe Morisot, Summer’s Day, 1879. Edgar Degas, L’Absinthe, 1875–1876. Georges Seurat, A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, 1884–1886. Michel Eugène Chevreul, chromatic circle illustrating the law of simultaneous color contrast, published 1839. PREVIOUS NEXT Looking at the Images Monet’s broken brushwork makes sunrise inseparable from the act of seeing it. Morisot treats figures, reflections, clothing, and water with an airy incompleteness; Degas uses cropping and social distance to make modern leisure feel uncomfortable rather than festive.
Seurat slows the passing instant into a calculated field of small color units. The color diagram matters because it shows that Pointillism is not simply a fussier version of Impressionism: it converts sensation into a system.
Impressionism begins from the instability of perception itself: changing light, modern movement, and the viewer’s situated glance. Pointillism retains that concern with perception but replaces spontaneous-looking touch with calculated optical mixture. It is one of several routes beyond Impressionism developed explicitly in Unit 30.
Featured Poems and Texts Impression du Matin
Oscar Wilde
First published in The World (1881)
The Thames nocturne of blue and gold
Changed to a Harmony in grey:
A barge with ochre-coloured hay
Dropt from the wharf: and chill and cold
The yellow fog came creeping down
The bridges, till the houses’ walls
Seemed changed to shadows, and St. Paul’s
Loomed like a bubble o’er the town.
Then suddenly arose the clang
Of waking life; the streets were stirred
With country wagons: and a bird
Flew to the glistening roofs and sang.
But one pale woman all alone,
The daylight kissing her wan hair,
Loitered beneath the gas lamps’ flare,
With lips of flame and heart of stone.

title: Lyric and Desire
content:
If Homer and Virgil presented the heroic, the epic, the historical, the mythological … and Keats and Rilke contemplated enigmatic objects of classical art and described their effects on the observer, Sappho gives us the intensely personal, the inner experience, the seemingly private — almost as if overheard.
Sappho and Erinna in a Garden at Mytilene by Simeon Solomon (1864) Fragment 31
Sappho, trans. Anne Carson
He seems to me equal to gods that man
whoever he is who opposite you
sits and listens close
to your sweet speaking
and lovely laughing—oh it
puts the heart in my chest on wings
for when I look at you, even a moment, no speaking
is left in me
no: tongue breaks and thin
fire is racing under skin
and in eyes no sight and drumming
fills ears
and cold sweat holds me and shaking
grips me all, greener than grass
I am and dead—or almost
I seem to me.
But all is to be dared, because even a person of poverty
Essential Questions Recall that Rilke seemed to indicate that the sculpture of Apollo surviving as ‘merely’ a fragment only intensifies its force. What of Sappho’s work itself surviving only in fragments? Why the strange grammar? “I am and dead.” “No: breaks and thin” leaves off. What could “greener than grass” mean? The fragment cuts off abruptly, just as seemingly a new line of thought began. Where do you think Sappho went next? Advanced Questions Show Hide Why say “I seem to me” rather than “I am”? Vocabulary Lyric — poetry of concentrated voice, feeling, perception, or inward experience. Lyric usually does not tell a long public story like epic; it gives shape to a speaker’s immediate state of mind or body.
Eros — desire, especially erotic or passionate longing. In Greek poetry, eros is not merely “romance.”
Additional Poems and Texts Poem 51
Gaius Valerius Catullus
Translated from the Latin by Charles Martin, from The Poems of Catullus (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1989).
To me that man seems like a god in heaven,
seems—may I say it?—greater than all gods are,
who sits by you & without interruption
watches you, listens
to your light laughter, which casts such confusion
onto my senses, Lesbia, that when I
gaze at you merely, all of my well-chosen
words are forgotten
as my tongue thickens & a subtle fire
runs through my body while my ears deafened
by their own ringing & at once my eyes are
covered in darkness!
Leisure, Catullus. More than just a nuisance,
leisure: you riot, overmuch enthusing.
Fabulous cities & their sometime kings have
died of such leisure.
For three stanzas Catullus closely follows Sappho. But then a dramatic departure. Martin translates the repeated Latin otium as “leisure,” but the Latin word carries a larger set of associations. It can mean freedom from public business, unoccupied time, retirement, idleness, or a life withdrawn from civic duties.
What clearer Romanization?
Teacher notes Show Hide Emphasis the lyrical focus on the intense inner experience.
If Homer and Virgil intended a city, a civilization as audience, here the audience feels to be somewhere between small and intimate to non-existent.
Fragment 31 is composed in, well, Sapphic Stanzas. The first thing to notice about these is:
Long line Long line Lone line Short line With the short fourth line uses to make some sort of turn, or compression, or pack some sort of punch. The three longer lines tend to build towards something, then the compressed fourth line wallops you with something, or collapses, reverses, deflates, etc.
Notice that Sappho does not simply instruct the (overhearing) audience that a feeling is intense or overwhelming. She careful describes, directly, an experience.

title: Modernism
content:
Unit plan
Purpose. Modernist difficulty becomes a response to historical rupture, cultural overload, broken traditions, and competing voices rather than an arbitrary refusal to communicate.
Visual plan. A restrained four-object sequence. Poetry should dominate the page; the visual material demonstrates editorial fracture, simultaneous text and image, and two paths into abstraction.
Featured Artwork T. S. Eliot, typescript of The Waste Land with Ezra Pound’s revisions, 1921–1922. Fragmentation and Abstraction 1 / 1
Sonia Delaunay and Blaise Cendrars, La Prose du Transsibérien et de la petite Jehanne de France, 1913. Kazimir Malevich, Black Square, 1915. Wassily Kandinsky, Composition VIII, 1923. PREVIOUS NEXT Looking at the Images The marked typescript of The Waste Land makes modernism’s fragmentation materially visible as revision, deletion, rearrangement, and collaboration. Delaunay and Cendrars design reading as a simultaneous visual journey rather than a conventional sequence of pages.
Malevich and Kandinsky show two different routes into abstraction: radical reduction to a nearly absolute sign, and an orchestration of geometric tensions that still suggests movement and musical relation.
Featured Poems and Texts The Waste Land
T. S. Eliot
Substantial selected passages from the 1922 text
April is the cruellest month, breeding
Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing
Memory and desire, stirring
Dull roots with spring rain.
Winter kept us warm, covering
Earth in forgetful snow, feeding
A little life with dried tubers.
Summer surprised us, coming over the Starnbergersee
With a shower of rain; we stopped in the colonnade,
And went on in sunlight, into the Hofgarten,
And drank coffee, and talked for an hour.
Bin gar keine Russin, stamm’ aus Litauen, echt deutsch.
And when we were children, staying at the archduke’s,
My cousin’s, he took me out on a sled,
And I was frightened. He said, Marie,
Marie, hold on tight. And down we went.
In the mountains, there you feel free.
I read, much of the night, and go south in the winter.
What are the roots that clutch, what branches grow
Out of this stony rubbish? Son of man,
You cannot say, or guess, for you know only
A heap of broken images, where the sun beats,
And the dead tree gives no shelter, the cricket no relief,
And the dry stone no sound of water. Only
There is shadow under this red rock,
(Come in under the shadow of this red rock),
And I will show you something different from either
Your shadow at morning striding behind you
Or your shadow at evening rising to meet you;
I will show you fear in a handful of dust.
Frisch weht der Wind
Der Heimat zu
Mein Irisch Kind,
Wo weilest du?
“You gave me hyacinths first a year ago;
“They called me the hyacinth girl.”
—Yet when we came back, late, from the Hyacinth garden,
Your arms full, and your hair wet, I could not
Speak, and my eyes failed, I was neither
Living nor dead, and I knew nothing,
Looking into the heart of light, the silence.
Oed’ und leer das Meer.
Madame Sosostris, famous clairvoyante,
Had a bad cold, nevertheless
Is known to be the wisest woman in Europe,
With a wicked pack of cards. Here, said she,
Is your card, the drowned Phoenician Sailor,
(Those are pearls that were his eyes. Look!)
Here is Belladonna, the Lady of the Rocks,
The lady of situations.
Here is the man with three staves, and here the Wheel,
And here is the one-eyed merchant, and this card,
Which is blank, is something he carries on his back,
Which I am forbidden to see. I do not find
The Hanged Man. Fear death by water.
I see crowds of people, walking round in a ring.
Thank you. If you see dear Mrs. Equitone,
Tell her I bring the horoscope myself:
One must be so careful these days.
Unreal City,
Under the brown fog of a winter dawn,
A crowd flowed over London Bridge, so many,
I had not thought death had undone so many.
Sighs, short and infrequent, were exhaled,
And each man fixed his eyes before his feet.
Flowed up the hill and down King William Street,
To where Saint Mary Woolnoth kept the hours
With a dead sound on the final stroke of nine.
There I saw one I knew, and stopped him, crying “Stetson!
“You who were with me in the ships at Mylae!
“That corpse you planted last year in your garden,
“Has it begun to sprout? Will it bloom this year?
“Or has the sudden frost disturbed its bed?
“Oh keep the Dog far hence, that’s friend to men,
“Or with his nails he’ll dig it up again!
“You! hypocrite lecteur!—mon semblable,—mon frère!”
Oread
H. D.
From Sea Garden (1916)
Whirl up, sea—
whirl your pointed pines,
splash your great pines
on our rocks,
hurl your green over us,
cover us with your pools of fir. Essential Questions Advanced Questions Show Hide Vocabulary Additional Poems and Texts W. B. Yeats, “The Second Coming.” Ezra Pound’s editorial correspondence with Eliot. Teacher notes Show Hide

title: Motion and Machine
content:
Unit plan
Purpose. Artists attempt to invent forms adequate to trains, automobiles, crowds, repeated movement, industrial force, and urban simultaneity. The unit also examines the dangerous conversion of speed and violence into aesthetic ideals.
Visual plan. A nine-image movement survey divided into three sections: the photographic analysis of movement, Italian Futurism, and parallel experiments outside Futurism.
Artworks and Images I. Recording Movement 1 / 1
Eadweard Muybridge, The Horse in Motion, 1878. Sequential photographs. Étienne-Jules Marey, chronophotographic study of a running man, late nineteenth century. PREVIOUS NEXT Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, first page of the English-language “Declaration of Futurism,” published in Poesia, vol. 5, no. 6, April 1909. Printed manifesto. Public domain. The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism Futurism announced itself not merely as a new artistic style but as an assault on inherited habits of thought. Marinetti praises danger, machinery, speed, aggressive action, and the modern industrial city. He presents the motorcar, locomotive, factory, steamship, and aeroplane as emblems of a world whose movement has rendered older standards of beauty obsolete.
The manifesto’s exhilaration is inseparable from its violence. Its celebration of war, destruction, misogyny, and contempt for historical culture should therefore be read critically. The document reveals both the revolutionary energy that inspired Futurist experiments in motion and simultaneity and the destructive ideology embedded within the movement from its beginning.
The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism
F. T. Marinetti
Selected from the English ‘Declaration of Futurism,’ published in Poesia, vol. 5, no. 6 (April 1909), following the manifesto’s appearance in Le Figaro, Paris, 20 February 1909. Spelling and punctuation lightly regularized. Public-domain text.
MANIFESTO OF FUTURISM
We intend to glorify the love of danger, the custom of energy, the strength of daring.
The essential elements of our poetry will be courage, audacity, and revolt.
Literature having up to now glorified thoughtful immobility, ecstasy, and slumber, we wish to exalt the aggressive movement, the feverish insomnia, running, the perilous leap, the cuff and the blow.
We declare that the splendour of the world has been enriched with a new form of beauty: the beauty of speed. A race-automobile adorned with great pipes like serpents with explosive breath—a race-automobile which seems to rush over exploding powder—is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace.
We will sing the praises of man holding the fly-wheel, of which the ideal steering-post traverses the earth, impelled itself around the circuit of its own orbit.
The poet must spend himself with warmth, brilliancy, and prodigality to augment the fervour of the primordial elements.
There is no more beauty except in struggle. No masterpiece without the stamp of aggressiveness. Poetry should be a violent assault against unknown forces, to summon them to lie down at the feet of man.
We are on the extreme promontory of ages! Why look back, since we must break down the mysterious doors of Impossibility? Time and Space died yesterday. We already live in the Absolute, for we have already created omnipresent, eternal speed.
We will glorify war—the only true hygiene of the world—militarism, patriotism, the destructive gesture of the anarchist, the beautiful Ideas which kill, and the scorn of woman.
We will destroy museums and libraries, and fight against moralism, feminism, and all utilitarian cowardice.
We will sing the great masses agitated by work, pleasure, or revolt; we will sing the multicoloured and polyphonic surf of revolutions in modern capitals; the nocturnal vibration of arsenals and docks beneath their glaring electric moons; greedy stations devouring smoking serpents; factories hanging from the clouds by the threads of their smoke; bridges like giant gymnasts stepping over sunny rivers sparkling like diabolical cutlery; adventurous steamers scenting the horizon; large-breasted locomotives bridled with long tubes; and the slippery flight of aeroplanes whose propellers have flag-like flutterings and the applause of enthusiastic crowds.
Having declared Futurism’s principles, Marinetti turns against Italy’s museums and its reverence for inherited culture.
It is in Italy that we hurl this overthrowing and inflammatory declaration, with which today we found Futurism, for we will free Italy from her numberless museums, which cover her with countless cemeteries.
Museums, cemeteries! Identical, truly, in the sinister promiscuousness of so many objects unknown to each other. Public dormitories, where one is forever slumbering beside hated or unknown beings. Reciprocal ferocity of painters and sculptors murdering each other with blows of form and colour in the same museum.
That a yearly visit be paid there, as one visits the grave of dead relatives once a year—we are ready to grant it! That an annual offering of flowers be laid at the feet of the Gioconda, we conceive it! But to take for a daily walk through museums our spleen, lack of courage, and morbid restlessness, we will not grant it! Why will you poison yourselves? Why will you decay?
What can one see in an old picture except the artist’s laborious contortions, struggling to overcome the insuperable barriers ever resisting his desire to express his entire dream?
To admire an old picture is to pour our sentiment into a funeral urn instead of hurling it forth in violent gushes of action and productiveness. Will you thus consume your best strength in this useless admiration of the past, from which you will forcibly come out exhausted, lessened, and trampled?
[…]
Marinetti distinguishes the young Futurists from those who seek consolation in the past and converts his rejection of cultural inheritance into an explicit fantasy of destruction.
But we will have none of it, we the young, the strong, the living Futurists!
Therefore welcome the kindly incendiaries with carbon fingers! Here they are! Here! Away and set fire to the bookshelves! Turn the canals and flood the vaults of museums! Oh! Let the glorious old pictures float adrift! Seize pickaxe and hammer! Sap the foundations of the venerable towns!
[…]
Art can only be violence, cruelty, and injustice.
Erect on the pinnacle of the world, we once more hurl forth our defiance to the stars!
II. Italian Futurism 1 / 1
Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises, 1910. Umberto Boccioni, States of Mind I: The Farewells, 1911. Giacomo Balla, Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash, 1912. Giacomo Balla, Abstract Speed + Sound, 1913–1914. Gino Severini, Armored Train in Action, 1915. PREVIOUS NEXT III. Parallel Experiments 1 / 1
Marcel Duchamp, Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2, 1912. Wyndham Lewis, Workshop, c. 1914–1915. PREVIOUS NEXT Looking at the Images Muybridge and Marey divide motion into measurable intervals. Futurist artists then reassemble movement as simultaneity: repeated limbs, radiating lines, compressed journeys, noise, crowds, and machines occupy the same image at once.
Duchamp and Lewis show that the problem of modern dynamism was not confined to Italian Futurism. At the same time, Severini’s armored train makes the unit’s political danger explicit: formal excitement can turn mechanized violence into spectacle.
Featured Poems and Texts The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism

title: Nature as Revelation
content:
Unit plan
Purpose. Nature becomes more than external scenery or overwhelming force. It appears as memory, symbol, moral presence, sacrament, or evidence of a reality perceived through imaginative attention.
Visual plan. A three-work progression from observed landscape to visionary landscape and explicitly symbolic creation.
Artworks and Images Observed and Visionary Nature 1 / 1
John Constable, The Hay Wain, 1821. Samuel Palmer, The Magic Apple Tree, c. 1830. William Blake, The Ancient of Days, 1794. Monochrome relief-etching impression of the design. PREVIOUS NEXT Looking at the Images Constable’s landscape grounds vision in observed weather, labor, water, and local place. Palmer makes the rural world denser and more visionary: moon, tree, field, and human figure seem charged with inward significance. Blake’s geometrical creator turns the act of measuring the universe into a symbolic image.
The progression moves from nature seen attentively, to nature transfigured by imagination, to a cosmos explicitly represented as spiritual design.
Featured Poems and Texts Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey
William Wordsworth
Text of Lyrical Ballads (1798)
Five years have past; five summers, with the length
Of five long winters! and again I hear
These waters, rolling from their mountain-springs
With a soft inland murmur. –Once again
Do I behold these steep and lofty cliffs,
That on a wild secluded scene impress
Thoughts of more deep seclusion; and connect
The landscape with the quiet of the sky.
The day is come when I again repose
Here, under this dark sycamore, and view
These plots of cottage-ground, these orchard-tufts,
Which at this season, with their unripe fruits,
Are clad in one green hue, and lose themselves
‘Mid groves and copses. Once again I see
These hedge-rows, hardly hedge-rows, little lines
Of sportive wood run wild: these pastoral farms,
Green to the very door; and wreaths of smoke
Sent up, in silence, from among the trees!
With some uncertain notice, as might seem
Of vagrant dwellers in the houseless woods,
Or of some Hermit’s cave, where by his fire
The Hermit sits alone.
These beauteous forms,
Through a long absence, have not been to me
As is a landscape to a blind man’s eye:
But oft, in lonely rooms, and ‘mid the din
Of towns and cities, I have owed to them,
In hours of weariness, sensations sweet,
Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart;
And passing even into my purer mind,
With tranquil restoration:–feelings too
Of unremembered pleasure: such, perhaps,
As have no slight or trivial influence
On that best portion of a good man’s life,
His little, nameless, unremembered, acts
Of kindness and of love. Nor less, I trust,
To them I may have owed another gift,
Of aspect more sublime; that blessed mood,
In which the burthen of the mystery,
In which the heavy and the weary weight
Of all this unintelligible world,
Is lightened:–that serene and blessed mood,
In which the affections gently lead us on,–
Until, the breath of this corporeal frame
And even the motion of our human blood
Almost suspended, we are laid asleep
In body, and become a living soul:
While with an eye made quiet by the power
Of harmony, and the deep power of joy,
We see into the life of things.
If this
Be but a vain belief, yet, oh! how oft–
In darkness and amid the many shapes
Of joyless daylight; when the fretful stir
Unprofitable, and the fever of the world,
Have hung upon the beatings of my heart–
How oft, in spirit, have I turned to thee,
O sylvan Wye! thou wanderer thro’ the woods,
How often has my spirit turned to thee!
And now, with gleams of half-extinguished thought,
With many recognitions dim and faint,
And somewhat of a sad perplexity,
The picture of the mind revives again:
While here I stand, not only with the sense
Of present pleasure, but with pleasing thoughts
That in this moment there is life and food
For future years. And so I dare to hope,
Though changed, no doubt, from what I was when first
I came among these hills; when like a roe
I bounded o’er the mountains, by the sides
Of the deep rivers, and the lonely streams,
Wherever nature led: more like a man
Flying from something that he dreads, than one
Who sought the thing he loved. For nature then
(The coarser pleasures of my boyish days,
And their glad animal movements all gone by)
To me was all in all.–I cannot paint
What then I was. The sounding cataract
Haunted me like a passion: the tall rock,
The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood,
Their colours and their forms, were then to me
An appetite; a feeling and a love,
That had no need of a remoter charm,
By thought supplied, nor any interest
Unborrowed from the eye.–That time is past,
And all its aching joys are now no more,
And all its dizzy raptures. Not for this
Faint I, nor mourn nor murmur; other gifts
Have followed; for such loss, I would believe,
Abundant recompence. For I have learned
To look on nature, not as in the hour
Of thoughtless youth; but hearing oftentimes
The still, sad music of humanity,
Nor harsh nor grating, though of ample power
To chasten and subdue. And I have felt
A presence that disturbs me with the joy
Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime
Of something far more deeply interfused,
Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns,
And the round ocean and the living air,
And the blue sky, and in the mind of man:
A motion and a spirit, that impels
All thinking things, all objects of all thought,
And rolls through all things. Therefore am I still
A lover of the meadows and the woods,
And mountains; and of all that we behold
From this green earth; of all the mighty world
Of eye, and ear,–both what they half create,
And what perceive; well pleased to recognise
In nature and the language of the sense,
The anchor of my purest thoughts, the nurse,
The guide, the guardian of my heart, and soul
Of all my moral being.
Nor perchance,
If I were not thus taught, should I the more
Suffer my genial spirits to decay:
For thou art with me here upon the banks
Of this fair river; thou my dearest Friend,
My dear, dear Friend; and in thy voice I catch
The language of my former heart, and read
My former pleasures in the shooting lights
Of thy wild eyes, Oh! yet a little while
May I behold in thee what I was once,
My dear, dear Sister! and this prayer I make,
Knowing that Nature never did betray
The heart that loved her; ’tis her privilege,
Through all the years of this our life, to lead
From joy to joy: for she can so inform
The mind that is within us, so impress
With quietness and beauty, and so feed
With lofty thoughts, that neither evil tongues,
Rash judgments, nor the sneers of selfish men,
Nor greetings where no kindness is, nor all
The dreary intercourse of daily life,
Shall e’er prevail against us, or disturb
Our cheerful faith, that all which we behold
Is full of blessings. Auguries of Innocence
William Blake
Selected lines; written c. 1803
To see a World in a Grain of Sand
And a Heaven in a Wild Flower,
Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand
And Eternity in an hour.
A Robin Red breast in a Cage
Puts all Heaven in a Rage.
A dove house fill’d with doves and pigeons
Shudders Hell thro’ all its regions.
A dog starv’d at his master’s gate
Predicts the ruin of the State.
A horse misus’d upon the road
Calls to Heaven for Human blood.
The wild deer wand’ring here and there
Keeps the Human Soul from Care.
The lamb misus’d breeds Public Strife
And yet forgives the Butcher’s knife.
